item.title: Switch Lowering in GCC (195 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://xoranth.net/gcc-switch/, See on Hacker News

Switch lowering in GCC

2024-01-14

Introduction

We have seen in a previous post that switch statements are more complex than they seem. The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't). Is that everything it can do?

In this post, I'll focus on gcc. All optimizations, except the bitset lowering, translate to clang. I'll be using the -O3 optimization flag unless indicated otherwise.

I've also slightly edited gcc code and removed certain assertions for brevity.

Examples

Let us start with a simple example. A function that takes two integers x and val. Depending on the value of x, it calls a corresponding function (f0, f1, and so forth) with val as an argument and returns the result. Were we to implement this manually, we'd would use an array of function pointers, where the input serves as the index into the array.

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);

int compact(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 0:
            return f0(val);
        case 1:
            return f1(val);
        case 2:
            return f2(val);
        case 3:
            return f3(val);
        case 4:
            return f4(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

compact:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 4
	ja	.L2
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]]
.L4:
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L6
	.quad	.L5
	.quad	.L3
.L5:
	jmp	f3
.L3:
	jmp	f4
.L8:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f1
.L6:
	jmp	f2
.L2:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret

The compiler agrees with this approach, and transforms the switch statement into a jump table.

Moreover, it is able to identify when the values are offset by a constant:

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);

int compact(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 97:
            return f0(val);
        case 98:
            return f1(val);
        case 99:
            return f2(val);
        case 100:
            return f3(val);
        case 101:
            return f4(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

compact:
	lea	eax, [rdi-97]
	cmp	eax, 4
	ja	.L2
	mov	edi, esi
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]]
.L4:
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L6
	.quad	.L5
	.quad	.L3
.L5:
	jmp	f3
.L3:
	jmp	f4
.L8:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f1
.L6:
	jmp	f2
.L2:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret

Our intuition suggests that the more sparse the values, the less advantageous the jump table conversion is.

Through experimentation, we find that gcc considers the threshold to be around eight jump table entries per case label.

In other words, the following function compiles to a jump table:

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);

int compact_7(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 0:
            return f0(val);
        case 7:
            return f1(val);
        case 14:
            return f2(val);
        case 21:
            return f3(val);
        case 34:
            return f4(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

compact_7:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 34
	ja	.L2
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]]
.L4:
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L6
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L5
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L3
.L2:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
.L8:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f1
.L6:
	jmp	f2
.L5:
	jmp	f3
.L3:
	jmp	f4

But this other function is expanded as a tree of comparisons:

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);

int sparse_8(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 0:
            return f0(val);
        case 8:
            return f1(val);
        case 16:
            return f2(val);
        case 24:
            return f3(val);
        case 40:
            return f4(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

sparse_8:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 16
	je	.L2
	jle	.L10
	cmp	eax, 24
	je	.L7
	cmp	eax, 40
	jne	.L1
	jmp	f4
.L10:
	test	eax, eax
	je	.L4
	cmp	eax, 8
	jne	.L1
	jmp	f1
.L1:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
.L4:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f3
.L2:
	jmp	f2

Here's the comparison tree visualized for clarity:

A couple of observations:

  1. We've only tried equally spaced values so far. Can the compiler identify transformations that are profitable on a subset of all cases?
  2. So far each case led to a different result. What if we had different cases with the same result?
  3. The switch in sparse_8 could be simplified by dividing x by eight before the jump. Interestingly, gcc doesn't find this simplification.

Let's dig into 1. and 2.

Outliers

Altering our first example by including an outlier value shows that the compiler is able to recognize dense subsets of cases.

int f0(int val);
int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);
int f5(int val);

int outlier(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 1:
            return f0(val);
        case 2:
            return f1(val);
        case 3:
            return f2(val);
        case 4:
            return f3(val);
        case 5:
            return f4(val);
        case 100:
            return f5(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

outlier:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 5
	jg	.L2
	test	eax, eax
	jle	.L1
	cmp	eax, 5
	ja	.L4
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L6[0+rax*8]]
.L6:
	.quad	.L4
	.quad	.L4
	.quad	.L9
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L5
.L2:
	cmp	eax, 100
	jne	.L1
	jmp	f5
.L7:
	jmp	f3
.L5:
	jmp	f4
.L9:
	jmp	f1
.L8:
	jmp	f2
.L4:
	jmp	f0
.L1:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret

The compiler emits a branch for case 100, but emits a jump table for case 1 through 5.

Contiguous

In our examples so far, each case statement lead to a different code block. Let's test what happens when multiple case labels invoke the same function.

int f1(int val);
int f2(int val);
int f3(int val);
int f4(int val);
int f5(int val);

int blocks_2(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case 0:  case 1:  case 2:  case 3:
            return f1(val);
        case 21:  ...  case 24:
            return f2(val);
        case 42:  ...  case 45:
            return f3(val);
        case 63:  ...  case 66:
            return f4(val);
        case 84:  ...  case 87:
            return f5(val);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

blocks_2:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 45
	jg	.L2
	cmp	eax, 41
	jg	.L3
	cmp	eax, 3
	jg	.L4
	test	eax, eax
	js	.L1
	jmp	f1
.L2:
	cmp	eax, 66
	jg	.L8
	cmp	eax, 62
	jle	.L1
	jmp	f4
.L4:
	sub	eax, 21
	cmp	eax, 3
	ja	.L1
	jmp	f2
.L8:
	sub	eax, 84
	cmp	eax, 3
	ja	.L1
	jmp	f5
.L3:
	jmp	f3
.L1:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret

We have 20 case labels, with values between 0 and 87. The compiler could lower this switch to a jump table with 88 entries. Our hypothesis for the heuristic is that a jump table conversion is profitable when its size is smaller than 8 * num_case_labels. Since 88 < 20 * 8, the conversion should be profitable in this case, however gcc opted to lower the switch to a sequence of comparisons.

To better understand why, let's examine a specific block of case labels.

int blocks_2(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
                case 42:  case 43:  case 44:  
        case 45:
            return f3(val);
            }
    return 0;
}

blocks_2:
	mov	eax, edi ; Move `val` to $eax
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 45
	; If val <= 45, do _not_ jump
	jg	.L2
	cmp	eax, 41
	; If val >= 42, jump to L3
	jg	.L3
	; ...
.L2:
; ...
.L3:
        ; We reach L3 only if 42 <= val <= 45
        jmp	f3        ; Call f3(val)
; ...

The compiler realizes that the cases are contiguous and can be implemented with two comparisons instead of four. If the input of the jump table heuristic is the number of comparisons instead of case labels, things work out:

We have a total of 10 comparisons. Since 10 * 8 < 88, our revised heuristic suggests that a jump table transformation is unprofitable.

Non-contiguous

Let us try a non-contiguous case.

int f1(int val);

int bittest(int x, int val) {
    switch (x) {
        case '0':  case '2':  case '4':  
        case '5':  case '7':  case '9':  
        case 'A':  case 'C':  case 'E':
            return f1(x);
        default:
            return 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

bittest:
	lea	eax, [rdi-48]
	cmp	eax, 21
	ja	.L1
	mov	edx, 2753205  ; ???
	bt	rdx, rax
	jc	.L7
.L1:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
.L7:
	jmp	f1

The compiler emits non-intuitive machine code. Why is there no cmp nor jump tables? Where does the constant 2753205 come from?

An hint comes from the instruction bt. According to the Intel docs, bt:

Selects the bit in a bit string (specified with the first operand, called the bit base) at the bit-position designated by the bit offset (specified by the second operand) and stores the value of the bit in the CF flag.

If we examine the binary representation of 2753205, we find that it is in fact a bitset. The bits that are set to one correspond to the ASCII values of the case labels, each value being reduced by 48.

Implementation

We've encountered several distinct lowering strategies employed by gcc. For a more in-depth understanding, we can delve into the compiler's source code.

The compiler pass that responsible for lowering switch statements is the (appropriately named) pass_lower_switch, which in turn calls analyze_switch_statement.

Since gcc source can be daunting to follow, I'll provide a step-by-step commented version below. Following this, I will break down each section to explain its functionality.

bool switch_decision_tree::analyze_switch_statement () 
{
    unsigned l = gimple_switch_num_labels (m_switch);
    auto_vec<cluster *> clusters;
     ...

    compute_cases_per_edge ();

Some preamble code. m_switch points to a gimple object. Gimple is the internal representation used by gcc. Through this, we extract the overall count of cases and the individual counts of cases for each outgoing edge.

We also allocate a vector that will record the lowering strategy chosen for each case label.

    for (unsigned i = 1; i < l; i++)
    {
        tree elt = gimple_switch_label (m_switch, i);
	// ...
        tree low = CASE_LOW (elt);
        tree high = CASE_HIGH (elt);

        profile_probability p
            = case_edge->probability.apply_scale (1, (intptr_t) (case_edge->aux));
        clusters.quick_push (new simple_cluster (low, high, elt, case_edge->dest, p));
        // ...
    }

More setup code. We notice that gimple has a concept of high and low value for each label. That is, contiguous case labels have already joined together at this stage.

For each case label, we allocate a simple_cluster. This cluster serves as a record, capturing the range of values associated with the label, the relevant output edge, and the likelihood of this cluster being chosen. This probability comes from profile-guided optimization. By default it is uniform among case labels.

    // ...
    vec<cluster *> output = bit_test_cluster::find_bit_tests (clusters);

We transform the vector of clusters we have created. The name bit_test_cluster hints to the bitset lowering strategy we saw before.

    /* Find jump table clusters.  */
    vec<cluster *> output2;
    auto_vec<cluster *> tmp;
    // ...
    
    for (unsigned i = 0; i < output.length (); i++) {
        cluster *c = output[i];
        if (c->get_type () != SIMPLE_CASE) {
            if (!tmp.is_empty ()) {
                                tmp.truncate (0);
            }
            output2.safe_push (c); 
        }
        else
            tmp.safe_push (c);
    }

This section allocates a vector for the transformed cases and a scratch vector. Any case that wasn't altered during the bitset transformation process is gathered in this scratch vector. These cases are then processed and cleared whenever we come across an optimized cluster.

Essentially, in this section we are looking for sequences of case labels that couldn't be converted into bitset clusters.

                vec<cluster *> n = jump_table_cluster::find_jump_tables (tmp);
                output2.safe_splice (n);
                n.release ();

We attempt to convert these consecutive labels into a jump table and add the outcome to the output.

    /* We still can have a temporary vector to test.  */
    if (!tmp.is_empty ()) {
        vec<cluster *> n = jump_table_cluster::find_jump_tables (tmp);
        output2.safe_splice (n);
        n.release ();
    }

This is a coda for the loop above.

    // ...

    bool expanded = try_switch_expansion (output2);
    release_clusters(output2);
    return expanded;
}

Whatever is left goes through another pass, which turns the switch statement into a decision tree. The bitsets and jump table are leaves of the decision tree.

Bitsets

Let's dig further into bit_test_cluster::find_bit_tests. The high level structure of the code is as follow.

Initially, we aim to find the optimal method to bundle all clusters into bitsets. Optimality, in this context, refers to minimizing the number of bitsets used. We do so using dynamic programming.

Subsequently, we iterate over the bitsets and apply a profitability heuristic. If the bitsets meet this heuristic, we emit a bit_test_cluster; otherwise, we keep the original simple_clusters.

vec<cluster *> bit_test_cluster::find_bit_tests (vec<cluster *> &clusters)
{
     ...

    unsigned l = clusters.length ();
    auto_vec<min_cluster_item> min;
     ...

    min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (0, 0, 0));
    for (unsigned i = 1; i <= l; i++)
    {
        
        min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (INT_MAX, INT_MAX, INT_MAX));

        for (unsigned j = 0; j < i; j++)
        {
            if (min[j].m_count + 1 < min[i].m_count
                    && can_be_handled (clusters, j, i - 1))
                min[i] = min_cluster_item (min[j].m_count + 1, j, INT_MAX);
        }

        gcc_checking_assert (min[i].m_count != INT_MAX);
    }

For the dynamic programming, we'll use a vector of min_cluster_item structures. Each min_cluster_item has three components:

  • The first records how many bitsets do we need to represent the first i case labels, where i is the index in the vector.
  • The second records the start of the last bitset.
  • The third is unused.

The dynamic programming is as follows. We want to find the minimum number of bitsets to represent the first i case labels.

The base case is straightforward, a single case label can be represented by a single bitset.

Suppose we have already have found the optimal number of bitsets for the first j case label, for all . We define to be the optimal number of splits for the first i elements. This means we already computed , and are now seeking .

If the range of case labels can be represented as a bitset cluster, it must be true that

Conversely, assume we have the optimal assignment for the first i labels. If the last bitset starts at label , this assignment is also optimal when restricted to . Were this not the case, we could improve the assignment on as well.

Therefore, it must be that:

These conditions are exactly what the if statement in the code above checks for.

The can_be_handled function controls whether a range of case labels can be turned into a bitset test. It tests two criteria:

  • The combined range of all the case labels must be smaller than the width of a register. On contemporary systems, the combined range should be less than 64.
  • The case labels must have at most 3 unique outgoing edges.

If there is more than one edge, we emit a cascade of bit tests.

    vec<cluster *> output;
    // ...
    
    /* Find and build the clusters.  */
    for (unsigned end = l;;)
    {
        int start = min[end].m_start;

        if (is_beneficial (clusters, start, end - 1))
        {
            bool entire = start == 0 && end == clusters.length ();
            output.safe_push (new bit_test_cluster (clusters, start, end - 1, entire));
        }
        else
            for (int i = end - 1; i >= start; i--)
                output.safe_push (clusters[i]);

        end = start;

        if (start <= 0)
            break;
    }

    output.reverse ();
    return output;
}

Now we convert only bitsets that satisfy the is_beneficial test. In the code count represents the number of case labels handled by the cluster, while uniq denotes the number of distinct outgoing edges.

bool bit_test_cluster::is_beneficial (unsigned count, unsigned uniq)
{
    return (((uniq == 1 && count >= 3)
              || (uniq == 2 && count >= 5)
              || (uniq == 3 && count >= 6)));
}

Jump tables

The logic for jump table conversion mirrors the one used for bit test conversion. It leverages dynamic programming to identify "clusters" that can be profitably converted to a jump table.

Let's delve into the code. 

vec<cluster *> jump_table_cluster::find_jump_tables (vec<cluster *> &clusters)
{
    if (!is_enabled ())
        return clusters.copy ();

    unsigned l = clusters.length ();
    auto_vec<min_cluster_item> min;
    min.reserve (l + 1);

We start by preallocating a vector of min_cluster_item. We'll use this vector to keep track of the best jump table assignments for consecutive case clusters.

    min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (0, 0, 0));

We also push the base case for dynamic programming. This corresponds to using a single jump table for the whole switch.

Let's focus now on the main loop.

    unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT max_ratio = /* Used in the main heuristic. See next snippet. */;
                
    for (unsigned i = 1; i <= l; i++)
    {
        // NOTE(xoranth): Base case
        min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (INT_MAX, INT_MAX, INT_MAX));
        
        /* Pre-calculate number of comparisons for the clusters.  */
        HOST_WIDE_INT comparison_count = 0;
        for (unsigned k = 0; k <= i - 1; k++)
        {
            simple_cluster *sc = static_cast<simple_cluster *> (clusters[k]);
             NOTE(xoranth): get_comparison_count is 2 for contiguous case 
             labels, and 1 otherwise
            comparison_count += sc->get_comparison_count ();
        }

        for (unsigned j = 0; j < i; j++)
        {
            unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT s = min[j].m_non_jt_cases;
            if (i - j < case_values_threshold ())
                s += i - j;
            
             Prefer clusters with smaller number of numbers covered.  
            if () 
            {
                                min[i] = min_cluster_item (min[j].m_count + 1, j,
					   s );
            }

            simple_cluster *sc = static_cast<simple_cluster *> (clusters[j]);
            comparison_count -= sc->get_comparison_count ();
        }
    }

The dynamic programming loop mirrors the one we used for bitsets. We want to find the minimum number of jump tables to represent the first i case labels.

We iterate over splits at the j-th case label, for j < i. During each iteration we track the best scoring split. The special case j == 0 represents a single jump table for the entire switch statement.

Inside this inner loop we also keep track of:

  1. How many distinct jump tables we would need to lower the switch.
  2. The start of the last jump table of the decomposition.
  3. How many cases cannot be handled by a jump table. In the code, this is the accumulator s.

Point 1. and 2. are analogous to the bitset lowering pass, while 3. is new and specific to jump tables.

Namely, there is some overhead to dispatching to a jump table, due to the indirect jump and the need to check bounds. Therefore gcc requires a minimum amount of case labels to generate a jump table.

If a split would generate a jump table that is too small, the size of the jump table is added to an accumulator s, which is used as a tie-breaker between different split candidates.

To compute the scoring, we need the comparison count between j-th and the i-th case label. We compute it summing up the number of comparisons for all labels, and decreasing the count as we progress in the inner loop.

We also need the number of unhandled case labels. We determine it comparing the size of the jump table to the result of the case_values_threshold function. This function is architecture dependent and takes into account the presence of switch-case specific instructions, but on modern x64 and Arm64 machines, it defaults to 5.

unsigned int default_case_values_threshold (void) {
    return (targetm.have_casesi () ? 4 : 5);
}

Let's now focus on the main heuristic, starting with how max_ratio is computed. I've reproduced below the main loop, omitting lines unrelated to the main heuristic.

We've seen in the examples section that gcc uses the ratio between jump table entries and comparisons as a metric for the lowering the heuristic. The code below shows that distinct ratios are used when optimizing for speed (flags -O[123|fast]) or size (flag -Os). Specifically, a ratio of 8 is used when optimizing for speed, while a ratio of 2 is used when optimizing for size.

    unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT max_ratio
        = (optimize_insn_for_size_p ()
                ? param_jump_table_max_growth_ratio_for_size    // This is `2`
                : param_jump_table_max_growth_ratio_for_speed); // This is `8`

    for (unsigned i = 1; i <= l; i++)
    {
        /* Set minimal # of clusters with i-th item to infinite.  */
        min.quick_push (min_cluster_item (INT_MAX, INT_MAX, INT_MAX));

        // NOTE(xoranth): Compute comparison count, see previous snippet

        for (unsigned j = 0; j < i; j++)
        {
             NOTE(xoranth): Compute unhandled cases, see previous snippet
            
             Prefer clusters with smaller number of numbers covered.  
            if ((min[j].m_count + 1 < min[i].m_count)
               || (min[j].m_count + 1 == min[i].m_count && s < min[i].m_non_jt_cases)
               && can_be_handled (clusters, j, i - 1, max_ratio, comparison_count)) 
            {
                min[i] = min_cluster_item (min[j].m_count + 1, j,
					   s  );
            }

            // NOTE(xoranth): Update comparison count, see previous snippet
        }
    }

Now onto the main loop. Given two splits, we prefer the one that results in fewer jump tables being emitted. Or, if they would result in the same number of jump tables, we prefer the one that handles the most case labels. We also ignore splits that would result in unprofitable jump tables, where profitability is checked by the can_be_handled function.

The can_be_handled condition, checks for overflow and compares the ratio of case labels to jump table entries:

bool jump_table_cluster::can_be_handled (const vec<cluster *> &clusters,
                                         unsigned start, unsigned end,
                                         unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT max_ratio,
                                         unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT comparison_count)
{
     If the switch is relatively small such that the cost of one
       indirect jump on the target are higher than the cost of a
       decision tree, go with the decision tree.

       [...]

       For algorithm correctness, jump table for a single case must return
       true.  We bail out in is_beneficial if it's called just for
       a single case.  
    if (start == end)
        return true;

    unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT range = get_range (clusters[start]->get_low (), clusters[end]->get_high ());
     Check for overflow.  
     ...

    return lhs <= max_ratio * comparison_count;
}

The coda of the function also mirrors the one for bitset clusters. It iterates over all jump tables in reverse order, and prunes the ones that fail the is_beneficial check.

    vec<cluster *> output;
    output.create (4);

    /* Find and build the clusters.  */
    for (unsigned int end = l;;)
    {
        int start = min[end].m_start;

        /* Do not allow clusters with small number of cases.  */
        if (is_beneficial (clusters, start, end - 1))
            output.safe_push (new jump_table_cluster (clusters, start, end - 1));
        else
            for (int i = end - 1; i >= start; i--)
                output.safe_push (clusters[i]);
        end = start;

        if (start <= 0) break;
    }

    output.reverse ();
    return output;
}

The is_beneficial check for jump tables aims to prune small jump tables. It compares the number of case labels to case_values_threshold.

bool jump_table_cluster::is_beneficial (const vec<cluster *> &, unsigned start, unsigned end) {
    if (start == end) return false;
    return end - start + 1 >= case_values_threshold ();
}

Binary tree

If gcc cannot emit a bitset cluster or a jump table, it falls back to a binary tree of comparison.

In emitting the tree, it takes into account the probability of each case label cluster. The probability can be obtained via profile-guided optimization, or with the __builtin_expect_with_probability builtin.

The code is pretty straightforward.

void switch_decision_tree::balance_case_nodes (case_tree_node **head, case_tree_node *parent) 
{
    case_tree_node *np = *head;
    if (np) {
        int i = 0;
        case_tree_node **npp, *left;
        profile_probability prob = profile_probability::never ();

Sum probability of all case labels.

        /* Count the number of entries on branch.  Also count the ranges.  */
        while (np) {
            i++;
            prob += np->m_c->m_prob;
            np = np->m_right;
        }

Split the case label list such that both halves have equal probability.

        if (i > 2) {
            npp = head;
            left = *npp;
	    // NOTE(xoranth): this divides prob by 2.
            profile_probability pivot_prob = prob.apply_scale (1, 2);

            while (1) {
                 Skip nodes while their probability does not reach that amount.  
                prob -= (*npp)->m_c->m_prob;
                if ((prob.initialized_p () && prob < pivot_prob) || ! (*npp)->m_right)
                    break;
                npp = &(*npp)->m_right;
            }

            np = *npp;
            *npp = 0;
            *head = np;
            np->m_parent = parent;
            np->m_left = left == np ? NULL : left;

Recurse in both halves to build the binary tree.

            balance_case_nodes (&np->m_left, np);
            balance_case_nodes (&np->m_right, np);
            np->m_c->m_subtree_prob = np->m_c->m_prob;
            if (np->m_left)
                np->m_c->m_subtree_prob += np->m_left->m_c->m_subtree_prob;
            if (np->m_right)
                np->m_c->m_subtree_prob += np->m_right->m_c->m_subtree_prob;
        } else {
	    // [...] Base case
        }
    }
}

Conclusion

We've seen the heuristics and lowering strategies gcc employs when compiling switch statements, including:

  • Compressing multiple case labels into a bitset.
  • Transforming the switch statement into a jump table.
  • Transforming the switch statement into a binary decision tree.

For anyone interested in delving deeper, I'd suggest examining the gcc source code, and reading this paper.

Finally, I want to thank B.X.V., C.P., and V.P. for their feedback when writing this post

Digital minimalism

For a long time I have been a fan of minimalism in my physical life: have few physical possessions, and try to do more with less. Four years ago, I wrote this blog post describing what I had in the 40-liter backpack that I travel around with.

Physical minimalism, however, was an idea that came of age in the 2000s and 2010s and was responding to the challenges and the opportunities of the 2000s and 2010s. I continue to believe that it is valuable - though I recognize some arguments in the other direction, notably that having the right kinds of physical things can make more practical to have more self-sovereignty over your life. But I also think that in the modern era, we need a new kind of minimalism: digital minimalism.

Digital minimalism is about being intentional about ways that you access digital technology, making each use a conscious choice rather than something that you get sucked into by default. In this post, I will describe some experiments that I've done in this direction.

Twitter (aka X) has always had a strain of toxicity to it, that has been increasing in recent years. The platform is definitely engaging, but it's often far from informative, and the ways in which it engages often do not make you feel good. But this all seemed to hit a particular crescendo for me around the end of 2024 and beginning of 2025. Many things were happening at that moment, but if you spent a lot of time on X you will likely remember a particular one: everyone seemed to be suddenly becoming fans of Adolf Hitler.

This is not even mentioning the time that Grok itself briefly turned into "MechaHitler".

Around the same time, "Crypto Twitter" was spiraling into a mood that I saw described as "financial nihilism": roughly, that the natural end state of blockchains is gambling, this is good, and if you dislike this and wish for something better then you are a stuck-up elitist prick.

Naturally, I had (and continue to have) my intellectual disagreements with both of these trends. But on top of that, I also started to more seriously pay attention to the fact that while the style of discourse on the platform was engaging, it was not enlightening and not making me feel good. And so for much of this year, I have been doing an experiment in distancing myself somewhat from this chaos. I did not leave X the platform, but I did leave X the interface. Instead, I have been doing most of my tweeting through Firefly:

Firefly is a multi-client that combines together X, BlueSky as well as Farcaster and Lens (both partially-Ethereum-based decentralized social media platforms). You can see tweets from all four platforms, and you can make a tweet that gets auto-posted to all four platforms.

My primary goal in doing this was to support decentralized social media, and to continue to engage with X but in a way that distributes network effect rather than locking it in. But in my months of using Firefly, I found that it also has a different effect: I feel much better using it.

I suspect the primary reason is that while Firefly allows you to tweet, and see other people's tweets, it is missing one central part of the X interface: The Algorithm™.

In particular, I suspect that in my time using the X interface, I fell into the following trap:

  1. See someone making a tweet supportive of Adolf Hitler.
  2. Click on the tweet and look around its quotes and responses, the same way that someone would morbidly stare at a car accident.
  3. The Algorithm™ thinks: "This user seems to be a fan of Adolf Hitler. Let me mark that down as one of his interests."
  4. See ten tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler.
  5. Click and look around with morbid curiosity, the same way that someone would morbidly stare if they saw for the first time a car accident where ten cars were crashed and burning at the same time.
  6. The Algorithm™ thinks: ... well, you get the idea.
  7. See a hundred tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler.

Now, in fairness to X and Elon and its hard-working employees, the Adolf Hitler fandom does seem to have greatly wound down in the one and a half years since then. I suspect part of this is because such movements inevitably burn out once people realize how immoral and stupid they are. But another part is undoubtedly genuine improvements in how The Algorithm™ works.

But even still, in those moments when I go back into the X interface, I find myself logging back out and going back to Firefly. I also find that my mind has changed. I find myself less interested in the various battles that the intellectual titans on the platform seem to be sucking every day of their lives into. Recently, I logged back in, and I learned that the culture war issue du jour was that people were stridently arguing about whether or not Mao was evil. When I saw this, I had an emotional response that was sort of similar to what I think is the common experience of being an adult, seeing some food or TV show or game that you used to love as a kid, and realizing that you now find no interest in it at all. I smiled, and immediately went back to enjoying my day.

My verdict: I recommend more people try this. Explore ways of greatly decreasing or scoping your social media use: use something like Firefly, access X only on Tuesdays, whatever works for you. Get the information benefits of the platform without getting sucked in to the vortex, which does operate on you in powerful subconscious ways that you may not realize.

Cell data minimalism

For a period of 100 days, I embarked upon a second experiment: I lived my life with my phone always on airplane mode. I still used wifi, but not my cell connection.

I had two goals in doing this:

  1. Privacy. A phone connected to cell is an always-on tracking device. Cell companies are notoriously bad at keeping that data secure, and sometimes they themselves sell it. So there is a large chance that a trail of your location will end up in the hands of intelligence agencies, military contractors, advertising companies, and more.

    Anonymous SIM cards are not a sufficient solution, for two reasons: (i) your phone can still be linked across its entire usage lifetime through its IMEI number, and (ii) you leak all kinds of data that can be used to reconstruct who you are from your fine-grained movement patterns, internet access patterns, and modern AI makes it very practical to uncover these patterns.

    Hence, the best location privacy solution is not having a cell connection at all (also, use GrapheneOS, and be very limited in what apps you give location permissions to; I had already been doing both).

  2. Mental health. Not having the internet at all for significant periods of time (when I'm outside) has been a good way of (re-)building the habit of surviving without it, and getting more mental peace and the space to think about other more healthy and productive things.

On the whole, I consider the experiment to have been a success. During those 100 days, I violated the "no cell data" rule once literally but not spiritually - I turned it on briefly to receive a confirmation code that I needed in order to maintain that phone plan itself, and once spiritually but not literally - when going on a remote and slightly dangerous hike, friends insisted that I bring along a few communication devices that they had for emergency comms and use them to check in once every few hours.

My largest inconvenience was a stretch of time I was in Singapore, when my inability to receive SMS confirmation codes meant that I could not log into Grab (the regional Uber equivalent). As a result, my food options were more limited, and I had to take the subway instead of a car even in situations where that was much more inconvenient.

Since those 100 days, I have opened the cell connection occasionally, but so far I have broadly continued an "airplane mode by default" lifestyle.

For navigation, I used CoMaps, a local-first mapping application that downloads OpenStreetMap data and then shows you a map, gives you directions to get where you need, etc locally. My general review of CoMaps is that I find it worse than Google Maps for navigating the human world (restaurants, stores, opening hours...) but better for navigating the natural-ish world (it knows about many trails that Google Maps does not, though it does occasionally fail by claiming trails that do not actually exist, leaving me on one occasion pushing through hundreds of meters of shrubbery to get back to civilization).

I also became interested in the concept of local world knowledge apps. In principle, the data size of meaningful packs of information about the whole world is not that large. Compressed English wikipedia (without media) is only 27 GB. OpenStreetMap's planet.asm is 2.2 TB, though you can doubtlessly prune that down to 1-10% of its size and have everything you might conceivably need.

This month there was a bounty (organized by Statuette; I contributed as one of the donors) to create local phone apps that try to make useful knowledge easily accessible offline.

Here are two of the apps:

Left: FieldAtlas. Right: Commonplace

My general impression is: right now, we are exactly on the cusp of these kinds of apps starting to make sense. Most of the participants in the competition were trying to use on-device text LLMs to think for a long time before coming up with an answer. My impression is that this approach was too slow: answering a single question would take anywhere from 1 to 22 minutes. The best apps, on the other hand, used some kind of semantic search to show the user a search result from the local database immediately, and then followed that up with a very small LLM writing a text answer. This gives actually-good answers in a very reasonable timeframe.

Finally, when you're out and about, especially if you have meetings, sometimes you do need to have internet when you're on the go. When you arrive at a place, you often need to contact a person you're meeting to confirm their exact location or to get them to open the door. When you're at one meeting, you often need to re-confirm details about the next. If you don't have cell data, your only option is public wifi - and importantly, the public wifi hotspot must allow you to connect without providing an SMS confirmation code.

Different places are very different in terms of how friendly they are. Here is a quick tier list, taken from places I've traveled to while I was paying attention to public wifi availability:

  1. Taiwan (or at least, the Taipei area)

    Taipei has a huge number of public wifi hotspots. When I opened my phone to check when walking outside (or even when inside an Uber), there was literally an over 25% chance that there was a hotspot I could connect to that was in range at that moment. Usually, these were either municipal government wifi, or public wifi run by local convenience store chains.

  2. Ukraine, USA, Canada, Singapore

    Ukraine was the most surprising for me. In a surprisingly large number of places, across multiple cities, there were open hotspots available, some of which did not even require a clickthrough. (If you're wondering if it's responsible for them to do this, given Ukraine's security needs, I suspect the answer is that they are primarily concerned about decreasing the enemy's internet access near the frontline and on drones flying at high speed through the air toward their cities, and street-level wifi is not really useful for either of those)

    USA, Canada and Singapore were all similar: they had a very high number of theoretically-public wifi hotspots in general, but a large portion of those hotspots were gated behind either SMS or some kind of login. But even still, a very significant number of open wifi hotspots were available.


    Also, I learned that Toronto has a fraternity (or sorority) that seems to be named after SBF.
  3. Austria, Hungary

    Both halves of Charles I's old empire are similar. There are many hotspots, but the great majority of the public ones require an SMS confirmation code to log in. I could find properly open wifi, but on several occasions it took trying quite a few hotspots and walking around for a while.

  4. Switzerland

    Despite its general reputation for privacy, Switzerland ranked at the bottom for me. Almost all public wifi hotspots require an SMS confirmation code. In my first 1.5 kilometers walking through the downtown, I found only two that do not: a random shoe store, and Starbucks, which lets you connect for 10 minutes, and then longer if you enter a confirmation code that you receive by email.

Web minimalism

Recently, I have been starting to do more and more things without relying on user interfaces inside of websites at all. The last few times I updated my IPFS hash on ENS, I did so through a command-line tool that an AI wrote for me. Many of the payments that I make through privacy protocols, I now make through the kohaku-cli tool.

Sending through kohaku-cli. Today, the CLI is even cleaner and easier to use; no need to specify the value twice and know what a tail call is.

Websites and web applications, especially web applications for doing crypto things, are dangerous for several reasons:

  1. If you access a web application, you end up re-downloading the application from the server thousands of times, and you are fully trusting the server each time. If the server gets hacked even one of the thousands of times that you open the site, you might be screwed. Regular old-fashioned applications (where you explicitly click "download") are better than this: you only need to trust the server to not be malicious or hacked at that exact moment once.

  2. Websites and web applications are by default very bad for privacy. When you access a website, it can see your browser (including version number), your operating system, your screen size, and once you start acting hundreds of other data points (eg. mouse movements, button click patterns) that quickly identify you. Websites often send user data (and metadata) to all kinds of third-party providers, from CDNs serving scripts to analytics companies, and this all happens by default.

  3. As we've seen with social media, web applications crafted by third parties with commercial interests may not have your interests at heart. Fine-grained UI decisions may be dark patterns optimized to extract, whereas what you want is bright patterns that are optimized to enlighten and educate and protect you.

So what's the alternative? Basically, bring back the Unix Philosophy, but make it better and much more user-friendly with local AI: speak English to tell your computer what to do rather than Bash.

At its core, the Unix philosophy was simple: make simple, modular tools that each do one thing and one thing well, and that are designed to talk to each other through the most universal interface (text). You as a user have extremely fine-grained choice about how to make the different programs fit together. UIs, on the other hand, combine many functionalities into one single opaque tool produced by a single developer. At their apex, UIs turned into "super-apps", which greatly concentrate power in the application developer and have complex and unintelligible internal workings, magnifying security risks. With LLMs, we can go back to the Unix philosophy approach, putting the fine-grained decision-making power back into the user's hands, but without the downside of everyone needing to become a programmer.

Conclusion

Physical-world minimalism, of the style that became popular in the 2000s and 10s, was made possible by a new wave of technology: computers and the internet. A single computer could substitute for dozens of physical things. As a result, you could live a life of much greater simplicity and freedom, with just a laptop, a few sets of clothing, and basic charging and hygiene equipment. Physical minimalism was much harder before the internet; it was doable, but would entail a much more complex lifestyle commitment. After the internet, the costs of a more physically minimalistic lifestyle greatly dropped.

With the last ten years of progress of software quality, together with modern AI, I would argue that we now have the wave of technology needed to similarly enable the next wave of minimalism: digital minimalism. We need social media less than before, because you can talk to the bot for information instead (and for human connection, there's still the old-fashioned solution: going out and talking to people in real life). We need the internet less than before, because there's so much more you can do purely locally and offline. And we need the web less than before, because you can do much more, and more conveniently, though either command-line tools or custom-made user interfaces, and AI can help you use or craft both. And these things are all happening at exactly the time that the flaws of these previous paradigms - and, for that matter, the flaws of using AI in the wrong way - are reaching their apex, and so a digital minimalism is becoming more and more necessary.

Each person's path to digital minimalism will be different, as each person has different needs. But I highly recommend everyone try reducing their digital clutter in at least one important way, and if you like the result then keep going.

Subject: Notice of Security Incident

This notice is being sent on behalf of Scribd, Inc., the parent company of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, by Epiq, Scribd Inc.’s notification partner.

Hello,

We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data.

We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details).

We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information.

Watch for phishing

We encourage you to stay vigilant for phishing attempts by bad actors pretending to be Scribd, Inc. or Scribd, Slideshare, Everand or Fable.

Remember that Scribd, Inc. will never ask you for your username and password or other sensitive information via email or text. If you did receive a message like that:

    Don't click on any links in it. Instead type scribd.com, slideshare.net, everand.com, or fable.co directly into your browser.
    Call us at: +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m., Central European Time.
    Report it through Scribd, Inc.'s Help Center.

For more information

We regret that this incident occurred and any concern it may cause you. If you have additional questions, contact the dedicated call center at +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m. Central European Time.

The National Cyber Security Center has helpful guidance on how to recognize and avoid phishing scams here.

What Scribd, Inc. is doing

    We have secured the affected system and ended the unauthorized access.
    We have notified law enforcement as well as the relevant data protection authorities.
    We are working with an expert third party cybersecurity firm to strengthen our access controls and monitoring.

We value the trust you place in us with your information, and don’t take that lightly. We are deeply sorry this happened and will keep you updated if anything further changes.

Scribd, Inc.
